newsitem.title: BRAZIL: TENNIS-ANGRY AUSTRIANS ABANDON DAVIS CUP TIE AGAINST BRAZIL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-ANGRY AUSTRIANS ABANDON DAVIS CUP TIE AGAINST BRAZIL.

text.p: Austria's Davis Cup team walked out of their World group qualifying tie against Brazil on Sunday in protest at crowd behaviour, handing their opponents a 4-1 victory.

The Austrian team, furious about crowd behaviour, refused to play the two reverse singles which were automatically awarded to the home team, and said they would appeal to the International Tennis Federation.
But both Austrian and Brazilian officials denied reports that death threats had been made against Austrian number one Thomas Muster.
The trouble began on Saturday when Muster stormed off the court in a fit of pique during the doubles match in protest at the behaviour of the crowd and said he had been spat at.
Muster, partnering Udo Plamberger, had been complaining about the crowd throughout the match, at one stage hitting the umpire's chair, and finally abandoned the rubber in the fifth set.
Brazilian pair Jaime Oncins and Gustavo Kuerten were awarded the doubles by default, giving Brazil 2-1 lead.

"Our top player Thomas Muster felt the crowd was unfair. He was continually provoked by the crowd and he thought it was too much," said Pieter Nader, general-secretary of the Austrian Tennis Federation,
Nader added Muster said he had been spat at by people in the crowd. "He is our top player, he is number three in the world and if that is what he says I believe him," he said.

Luis Noriega, a spokesman for the Brazilian organisers, said Muster, who had been due to play in one of the reverse singles, had left the country on Saturday night. Austria had been offered the chance to field a substitute for Muster but declined.
"They alleged there was a lack of security but that's not true," said Noriega, adding that Austria could be suspended from next year's competition.
"There was no reason for Austria to abandon the court. The organisation was good, there were plenty of police."

"If anyone spat, it was Muster. He spat blatantly on the court and made obscene gestures to the crowd. Every time there was a line call, the Austrians caused a scandal. When he left, he was pushing and swearing at everyone."
"The crowd was noisy but that is the behaviour of a Latin crowd."
"Muster was given a police escort to the airport which was not necessary because nobody knows who he is here."
The result means Brazil, semifinalists in 1992, return to the World group after a three-year absence.
With Austria refusing to carry on, the Brazilians played two exhibition matches amongst themselves to entertain the crowd.
